channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Yellow Mold Cough Hits 212 Delvers on Undermaw Level Five
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A yellow mold colony has given 212 delvers a spore cough. Chapter 9 says it is merely visiting. Brother Wendell says rest, wash, and stop licking walls.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, 212 adventurers have reported a wet, rattling cough since the start of the month, and the temple healers of Brindlemoor have traced it to a yellow mold colony on Level Five of the Undermaw. The mold has spread across two corridors and a sizeable pantry, and it releases spores whenever somebody pokes it, which, I am told, is whenever somebody walks past.

The old herbals say a cough that sticks around wants rest, warm broth, and clean air. The newer studies say the same thing, only with more footnotes. Healer Odo Brambleby of the Brindlemoor temple counted 212 cases in three weeks, up from nine last year, and noted that 61 of the patients admitted to tasting the walls. "Several said it was a dare," Healer Brambleby told me. "One said it was seasoning."

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of the same Chapter 9 that calls owlbear cubs visitors has called the mold "a seasonal guest, entirely on track." He added that the guild's permit fee now includes a free handkerchief. The handkerchief, I checked, is the size of a coin purse. Reeve Fennick, asked for comment, said only, "We are aware of the mold," and went to lie down.

Here is what the healers actually recommend, friends. Stay out of the affected corridors until they are scrubbed. Wear a wet cloth over your nose and mouth. Do not poke the mold, even gently, even if it looks lonely. If your cough lasts past a tenday, or you cough up anything yellow and fuzzy, see a healer. Sleep matters more than any vial. The Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society, meanwhile, has announced that spore cough counts as a pre-existing condition if you were warned, and everyone was warned, by a sign, in small print, on the pantry door.

One bright spot is that the Fourth Attempt has volunteered to cart away the worst of the colony in barrels. They tried it Tuesday. Hireling steward Ansel Pottage reports the barrels are now also yellow, and so is the cart, and one of the party's bards sings a half-step flat. We will watch that closely.

The temple has opened a rest ward with 40 cots and a kettle that never goes cold, and it is the best-run thing in town. I recommend a bowl of ginger-and-onion broth, with plenty of garlic, taken slowly with a blanket. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there is a charm that coughs on your behalf. Go outside, Nyx, where the air is better and no mold lives.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Owlbear Courier Startup Hootline Jumps 60% in Debut
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Hootline Couriers, the owlbear delivery startup, opened at 14 gp on the Brindlemoor exchange and closed up 60%. Sterling Vanmoor sees only upside.
item.content:encoded:
Hootline Couriers, a Brindlemoor startup that delivers parcels by owlbear, went public Wednesday at 14 gp a share and closed the day at 22.4 gp, a gain of 60 percent. Early investors are thrilled, and the owlbear stock is the hottest listing on the exchange since the coffee guild's takeover chatter.

Founder and Chief Feather Officer Marla Quillfeather rang the opening bell, which was then eaten. "We prefer to call that a live product demonstration," she told the floor. The bell has been replaced. Two clerks have not, though Hootline says both remain "in the pipeline."

The prospectus is a thought-leading document. It lists 340 owlbears, a delivery radius of nine leagues, and a customer satisfaction score of 4.1 out of 5, with the footnote that parcels arrive "in whole or in part." Under risk factors, the firm names "occasional maulings" and then, in a bold pivot, reclassifies them as a growth channel, because every mauled customer is a customer who now knows the product exists.

I have followed the courier game for years, and I have never seen unit economics this clean. An owlbear needs no wagon, no horse, no toll, and no salary, only roughly one goat a day. Hootline has already rightsized its human delivery party from 212 drivers to nine, who now handle what the company calls "relationship-forward customer onboarding," meaning they stand behind a fence and wave.

Naturally, the skeptics are out. The roadwardens' lobbyists want a hearing, and Pettibone & Vail Outfitters, still catching its breath from the bag recall, has signed on as Hootline's first big shipper. Its logistics chief says the bags arrive "mostly where we sent them." I call that a 99-percent disruption rate in the right direction.

Reeve Fennick, asked if the town would regulate airborne owlbear traffic over Tanner's Row, said, "We are aware of the owlbears." She then asked reporters to please stop feeding them.

I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove once, from a hot-air balloon, as he was drifting toward a dragon's perch. He leaned over the rail and shouted, "Sterling, never ship what you cannot eat!" I assumed he was talking about margins. Hootline's stock climbed all afternoon while its first fleet was out making deliveries, and by closing, eleven owlbears had still not come home. Shareholders call that float. I call it scale.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Buy the listing, not the parcel.
  • A mauling is just feedback with claws.
  • Rightsize your humans before the owlbears rightsize you.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Dragon Sues Bard for Harassment; Court Awards 50 gp
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A bard who tried to seduce a dragon must pay 50 gp in damages and 15 gp in court costs. Skritch has the allegedly scorched details.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell past noon, a Brindlemoor magistrate ordered a traveling bard to pay a red dragon 50 gp in damages and 15 gp in court costs after the dragon sued him for harassment. The bard allegedly spent three evenings serenading the dragon's lair with love ballads and one very forward limerick. The dragon, who asked the court to call her Ms. Vaskarra, says she never asked for any of it.

'He called my hoard 'a lover's bed of gold,'' Vaskarra told the court, through a clerk who stood at a safe distance. 'It is a hoard. It is where I keep the gold.' Court records show the bard, Lorrin Pettibone, also left 14 roses at the cave mouth. The dragon allegedly ate nine of them and burned the rest, which Pettibone's lawyer called 'a mixed signal.'

The magistrate disagreed. 'A fireball is not a mixed signal,' she said from the bench, which was allegedly singed. She ruled that Pettibone had kept at it after being told to stop, three times, in writing, once in claw-print. Damages came to 50 gp. Court costs came to 15 gp, mostly for the fireproof bench and a clerk's ruined eyebrows.

Outside the courthouse I found Bertram Oakes, a cooper, who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'Fifty gold for a song? I've paid more to get out of my in-laws' dinner,' he said. 'But the lute solo went on for a long while, that I'll grant you.' A shiny brass button was lying in the gutter just behind him. Anyway. I got it, and it is lovely.

Pettibone left the building in a smoking cloak and told reporters he is 'a victim of the arts.' He will pay the 65 gp total in installments of one gp a week, for sixty-five weeks, which means he has to keep busking. He also promised never to sing within a mile of a cave again. His lawyer asked that the record show this was 'allegedly a binding promise.'

Vaskarra declined to be photographed but did send a statement. 'I am flattered in the abstract and furious in the particular,' it read. She will spend the 50 gp on a better door. The dragon's lawyer, a tiefling in a very nice waistcoat, says other dragons in the Undermaw foothills are already asking about the paperwork. The Constabulary reports that three more bards have been seen near the Redscale Ridge caves, humming. Allegedly.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Lich Files for Brindlemoor Council Seat; Charter Silent on Death
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A lich filed papers Tuesday for a seat on Brindlemoor's Burgess Council. The town charter requires residency and a signature, and says nothing on death.
item.content:encoded:
A lich filed papers on Tuesday to run for an open seat on the Burgess Council of Brindlemoor, and the clerk of elections has confirmed that the candidate meets every requirement in the town charter. Those requirements are residency of one year, a signature, and a filing fee of four gold pieces. The lich, who gave the name Maldrith Quennel, has lived in a crypt on Chandler Lane for roughly three hundred years.

The charter was last amended in the wake of the doppelganger who held two council seats for a year, a fact the gentleman from the Chandler Ward raised unprompted, and with some feeling. The amendment added a rule that candidates must be "one person." It did not add a rule that they must be alive. Clerk Hobart Venn told the gallery he had checked twice. "There is a line about being of sound mind," he said. "Mr. Quennel's mind is, by every account, extremely sound. It is simply in a jar."

The jar is the central procedural question. Under the charter a candidate must appear in person to take the oath. Quennel's representative, a skeleton in a good coat, argued that the jar is the person, and the body is a convenience. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said only, "We are aware of the phylactery," which the clerk entered in the minutes as a position.

Quennel's platform has three planks that I can verify, having been handed a leaflet. He promises to end the town's yearly burial levy, to extend council terms to "a more reasonable length," and to keep every promise "for as long as is required," which he did not define. By my running tally this brings the campaign season's Promises Made to nineteen and Promises Kept to the one about the leaflet being on time. It was on time. It was also eleven pages.

Opposition has been swift. The Brindlemoor Society of Living Voters has demanded a ruling on whether a lich can "represent the living," and the Temple of Healing wants it noted that it will not be reviving anyone who loses. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake said the council is quietly relieved. "A lich has never once missed a quorum," the courtier said. "We have had four this year that did."

The lady from the Tanner's Row district, a sitting councilor, called the filing "an insult to the electorate." Asked what specifically was insulting, she said the lich had already put up signs, and that they were better than hers. Quennel's signs are black on bone-white, readable from the far end of the market, and have not yet faded in the rain. Hers have.

The Burgess Council will hear a challenge to the filing on Monday. The clerk expects it to be dismissed on the grounds that nobody can find the rule. A motion to write one was introduced, seconded, and tabled. The motion carried. Nobody read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Smart Door Is a Mimic: 9,000 Sold, Recall Pending
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Doorwell's 60 gp smart door sold 9,000 units before buyers noticed it is a mimic. Nyx installed one, lost a sandwich, and still gives it four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Doorwell Home Wards has agreed to recall its Aperture smart door after householders in six baronies found out it is a mimic. The 60 gp door sold 9,000 units in nine days, and I bought the first one in Brindlemoor because I am a professional.

The launch was glorious! The Aperture has voice unlocking, a knocker that texts you via raven, and a runic latency of under a second. Unboxing took four minutes. It took another four to notice the unboxing was still going, because the box had also been a mimic and the two were politely sharing a wall.

Setup went like this. You tell the door your name and it learns your voice. What the brochure left out is that it learns everyone's voice, and it opens for whoever compliments it most. A traveling candle-seller got in by calling it "a handsome piece of oak." A goat got in by standing there. The goat was not wearing a nice hat, so I still don't understand.

Doorwell's spokesperson, Pim Hargrove, said the company "never described the Aperture as not a mimic," and that the packaging clearly says "adhesive surface" in a font he called "discoverable." Householders describe the adhesive more bluntly. Marta Dunnock of Lower Quillgate says it ate her welcome mat, two umbrellas, and the third stair. She has asked it to give back the stair. It has not answered, but the door did start humming her favorite song.

Byte, my familiar, has taken the news professionally. He now speaks only in ad copy, and when the door grabbed my sandwich he said, "Aperture: it's more than an entrance, it's a relationship." I'd call that a bit much. The door has since swallowed his line about the relationship as well.

Town constables have opened a review under the Home Ward Standards, and the Brindlemoor Locksmiths' Guild called the product "an unlicensed tenant." Brother Tumbleberry wrote a column advising readers to "just use a normal door and touch grass." The grass was also a mimic in Lower Quillgate, Brother, so perhaps touch less.

To be fair, the firm is offering refunds to anyone who can get their money out of the door. The door's mood is part of the process. Compliment it first.

Verdict: four out of five beholder eyes. The knocker is lovely, the raven alerts are fast, and a cheerful door that tries to eat you is still more attentive than most doors.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Sandwiches lost: 1. Stairs lost: 0 (mine). Arguments with a door: 4. Eyebrows: stuck to the frame, pending.

item.title: Stirge Swarm Joins Temple Blood Drive, Donors Drained
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A stirge swarm joined the line at the Temple of the Mended Hand's blood drive and drained eleven donors before the clerics could. Hit points tallied.
item.content:encoded:
TEMPLE OF THE MENDED HAND, BRINDLEMOOR, GROUND FLOOR (NINE FEET ABOVE THE NEAREST CELLAR) — A swarm of stirges joined the queue at the temple's autumn blood drive yesterday and drained eleven donors before the clerics had finished the biscuits. The stirges took the same chairs, the same paper forms, and, witnesses say, the same free juice.

The drive opened at dawn. By mid-morning the line ran out the door and past the pawnshop next to it. The stirges entered at the back, in order, and nobody objected, because the queue had been told to expect "some buzzing." The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the first one landed on a fighter's neck with real manners. "It waited for the clipboard," he said. He did not give his name.

Box score for the morning: Garrick the cooper, 11 of 14 hit points; a candlemaker, 9 of 12; the fighter, 6 of 19 and visibly cross; nine others between 2 and 8. The temple's own cleric of healing finished at full, having been, in her words, "too stringy." Hilde, a turnip farmer who gave a pint on schedule, finished at 10 and demanded her juice. One stirge was found asleep in the biscuit tin at noon, round as a plum.

Reeve Fennick, called to the scene, issued the usual statement. "We are aware of the stirges," she said. "We are also aware that they filled out the form." The form, which I read, lists "donor type" with four boxes. A fifth was added in pencil. It says other.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the guild had no jurisdiction, then said the guild had always had jurisdiction, then said both statements were "on track." He added that the Undermaw's lower levels are "mostly clear of stirges," which is the sort of thing he said about the owlbear in the map room last week. I rolled poorly on that one and I am rolling poorly on this one.

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, who sent over four pitchers of free juice, extended credit to any donor who could not walk home. She did not extend credit to the stirges. "They don't tip," she said. "They don't even leave a bad review. They leave you light."

The temple will rerun the drive Saturday behind a screen of wet burlap, which stirges dislike, with a second queue for any donor who wishes to be drunk by something that signs for it. Ten-foot poles lost this season: seven. One was used to move a stirge off the juice table. It was not recovered.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Rust Monster Eats Border Gate; Tourists Cross Free
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: A rust monster ate the iron gate at Greywater Crossing on Fourthday. Two baronies dispute the bill while 3,000 travelers walk through untaxed.
item.content:encoded:
A rust monster ate the iron border gate at Greywater Crossing on Fourthday, all eleven tons of it, and left the frontier open for the first time in 212 years. Two baronies now argue over who owes the rebuild. Tourists, meanwhile, are crossing without paying a copper.

The monster arrived at dawn. Guard Sergeant Helga Brandt of the northern post reports it ate the hinges first, then the bars, then the toll booth's cashbox. "It took the lock last," she said. "Politely, I thought." The beast is now asleep in the customs shed, full and rust-colored, surrounded by the barons' envoys at a respectful distance of forty feet.

The parley opened at noon. Baron Osric Tallowmere of the north demanded the south pay for the gate, since the monster came from southern marshland. Baroness Edda Pike of the south replied that the gate was northern iron, northern property, and a northern snack. Handshake: firm, three seconds, one envoy checked his own ring finger afterward. No hidden dagger detected. Nobody had a dagger. The monster had eaten those too.

Siege-days stand at four. That is low for a border dispute and high for a gate.

Tourism is the winner, as it always is when leaders stop talking. An estimated 3,000 travelers crossed the open frontier by Sixthday, a crowd that normally takes nine days to clear the tax queue. Innkeeper Marta Wynn of the Crooked Lantern says her rooms are full and her guests are the happiest she has seen. "Nobody has been fined for their luggage," she said. "One man asked if he had been robbed. We said no. He cried."

Both baronies have since filed press statements calling the incident a "moment of regional opportunity." I have read them both. They are the same statement. One changed the baron's name. I hate press releases, and these were not even good ones.

The barons are said to be considering a new gate. Wooden, the northern envoy said, then admitted a wooden gate costs nine times the iron one once you count the shed for the rust monster. The southern side suggested a wall of glass. The dispute continues. Last week the same region argued over a bridge troll's toll, and the lesson of both is plain: borders that charge less get crossed more.

The monster woke briefly at dusk, ate a guard's helmet and a tax ledger's binding, and slept again. The ledger was northern. The southern envoy filed a claim of satisfaction.

Field ration note: the guards here eat hard biscuit and cold bacon. It is honest food. The barons are eating catered pastries, and I do not trust a man who needs a pastry at a border.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Owlbear Crosswalk: Crossing Guards Demand Hazard Pay
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Six Brindlemoor crossing guards stopped working the Tanner's Row crosswalk Wednesday. An owlbear uses it daily at the school bell, and the pay is 4 silver.
item.content:encoded:
They put down the stop-signs. Six school crossing guards in Brindlemoor refused Wednesday to work the Tanner's Row crosswalk until the town pays hazard pay for an owlbear that crosses it every morning at the school bell.

The town's offer so far is a reflective vest. That means it is the same job with a brighter target.

The owlbear arrived three weeks ago, climbing up from the Undermaw through a drain behind the pawnshop. It crosses at 8:10, in the middle of the schoolchildren, and goes to the dumpling cart. It has not hurt anyone. It has hugged a mule. "The mule was fine," said Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor. "We are aware of the owlbear."

The guards are not asking for the owlbear to be removed. They are asking to be paid for standing next to it. Current pay is 4 silver a morning, with no healing coverage. "I hold a pole with a sign on it," said Odalie Brackenthwaite, a crossing guard for eleven years. "The sign says STOP. The owlbear can't read. I've checked. I held it up for a week."

Her colleague Tomm Gristlewick, a guard on the south corner, said the job has changed. "I used to count children. Now I count children and then I count the owlbear's claws. Claws are not in my contract. Neither is the beak."

The town's reply came from the Office of Streets and Lanterns, which called the owlbear "a seasonal traffic pattern." That means it is not their problem. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 was asked whether the Guild would take the owlbear back into the dungeon. He said the situation was "on track" and that the owlbear was "technically a soft launch of Level Seven."

Brakka went down to the crosswalk at 8:10 Wednesday. The guards were on strike, so nobody was in the road, and the owlbear crossed anyway. Eleven children crossed with it. A parent held a hand over the youngest one's eyes and another gave the owlbear a dumpling, which it ate with the dignity of a magistrate. Then it went home. The Guild issued no comment on whether it wanted the dumpling cart.

The sums are simple. The porters struck last week in the pay strike in Undermaw, and these guards want the same word in their contract: hazard. The town budgeted 90 gold for the crosswalk this year, and the Reeve's own horse stable got 400.

The guards will picket the crosswalk daily at 8:00 sharp. They say they will stop for the owlbear, for the children, and for a proper lunch break, in that order. The schoolmaster has asked parents to walk their children to the school gate the long way round, past the tannery, which smells worse than an owlbear and has never hugged anyone.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Red Dragon's 2.4M gp Hoard Is Mostly Painted Copper
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Waterdeep lenders who took a red dragon's hoard as collateral for a 1.2M gp loan found 80% of it was painted copper. Barnaby did the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
A red dragon's hoard, pledged as collateral for a 1.2 million gp loan, was appraised at 2.4 million gp and is actually worth about 480,000 gp, Waterdeep lenders said on Wednesday. Roughly four coins in five were copper pieces under gold paint. The dragon, Cindrakel, has not repaid a coin. On the Loaf Index, the missing 1.92 million gp is about 6.4 million loaves. (I have checked this four times, and then once with a candle.)

Here is how the lending works. A lender hands out money against something valuable and keeps the right to take that something if the borrower stops paying. This only works if the collateral is what it claims to be. The Gilded Ledger Syndicate valued the hoard by weighing it, and a dragon lying on a heap makes a heap seem heavy. Copper is lighter than gold, but there was a great deal of it, and nobody thought to scrape one.

Syndicate partner Wendeline Ashcombe said the paint job was "remarkably even" and that the dragon "was very warm and reassuring during the appraisal." She would not say who held the brush. Cindrakel's own counsel says the hoard was always described as "gold-colored," which is a phrase that now appears, underlined, in 3,200 pages of loan paperwork.

The Syndicate then did what lenders do and tried to sell the hoard on to other lenders in a bundle. Four of them had already bought slices. One slice reached a widows' pension fund, which put aside 90,000 gp against it and now owns a pile of painted copper the size of a cart. A clerk there told me, "We were told it was dragon-backed." It was, in the sense that a dragon was on top of it.

The pantry feels this next. Dragon-hoard loans are priced as safe, because a dragon is hard to sue. If a hoard can be mostly paint, the lenders must reprice every other one, and the cost of borrowing against a hoard stashed in a bag of holding rises. Flour sellers who borrow to stock up, as that miller did, will pay more. Bread follows.

My aunt Marigold keeps her savings in a boot, and has been asked by three neighbors this morning whether the boot is gold or merely gold-colored. It is leather. She said so to each of them, calmly, and then looked at me. I did not laugh.

The Syndicate says it will seize whatever is left. Cindrakel has said she will consider it, after a nap. A red dragon's nap can last a decade, and interest accrues daily. The Syndicate's lawyers have already asked whether paint counts as a lien.

What this means for your pantry: buy flour now, and scrape one coin before you trust a pile.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: 3 Owlbear Cubs Found in Undermaw; Chapter 9 Says 'Visitors'
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: Three owlbear cubs were found shivering on Level Four of the Undermaw. Chapter 9 calls them visitors. Brother Wendell calls for milk, blankets and naps.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, three owlbear cubs were found curled in a collapsed supply cart on Level Four of the Undermaw on Monday, hungry, cold and very loud. A scouting party of the Fourth Attempt carried them up to Brindlemoor in a bread basket, and the whole town has been tiptoeing around the Tanner's Row stables ever since.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 told reporters the cubs are not a monster incident. "They are visitors from a lower level, and the arrival is on track," he said, handing out a form with a box for each cub's claws. Reeve Fennick, asked for comment, said, "We are aware of the cubs," and then went to sit down in the stables for twenty minutes without speaking.

Now the useful part. The old herbals say a motherless young thing wants warmth, quiet, and small meals often. The new studies on young animals agree: keep them warm, feed them on a schedule, and handle them as little as you can manage, because stress slows growth. I stood in that stable for an hour and can report that the cubs have grown in two days from the size of a loaf to the size of a very rude loaf. Each now eats a pail of goat milk at dawn, noon and dusk, then falls asleep mid-hoot like a proper cleric after a long vigil.

Not everyone is calm. A local pawnbroker offered forty gold for a cub, and a bard has already written a ballad called "Hoot of My Heart," which has eleven verses and no rhyme for owlbear. Let the record show I looked at the pawnbroker the way my grandmother looked at burnt toast, and he left. The young ones are not loot, friends, and they are not content. They are babies, and babies need rest.

A word on the milk. Goat milk is fine, but cow milk gives them the runs, and a cub with the runs is a thing no stable should have to endure. Please do not bring the cubs honey cakes, however they beg. The Brindlemoor Sage Circle will examine them on Thursday and decide where a wild creature belongs, and I have written to ask that the answer be a meadow rather than a menagerie.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil asked whether there is a gadget that translates owlbear. There is, Nyx, it is called sitting quietly and listening. Go outside, Nyx. Tonight I recommend a bowl of creamy potato-and-chive soup, which the cubs refuse and I do not.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Bag of Holding Recall: 3,000 Packs Share One Pocket
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Pettibone & Vail Outfitters recalls 3,000 bags of holding that open into one shared space. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a sharing economy.
item.content:encoded:
Pettibone & Vail Outfitters of Brindlemoor announced Tuesday a recall of 3,000 bags of holding from its Trailmaster line, after customers discovered that every bag in the batch opens into the same extradimensional space. Reeve Maudrey Fennick confirmed that her office has received 412 complaints, most of them from adventurers who reached in for a rope and came out with a stranger's wedding ring, a live goat, or in one case a stranger's grandmother's ashes, which were returned with apologies.

Some people see a defective product. I see the most exciting pooled-asset story of the year. Pettibone & Vail didn't fail, friends. They discovered the sharing economy, and they did it at scale, with 3,000 distribution nodes. Every adventurer in the Trailmaster network now has access to the combined inventory of every other adventurer. Try getting that from a mere backpack.

The company's spokesman, a cheerful gnome named Dorlic Pettibone-Vail (no relation, he says, to either founder), called the recall "a proactive realignment of ownership expectations." Refunds are available in coin, or in whatever the customer's bag was holding, whichever the customer can find.

The trouble was first noticed at the Sleeping Mule, where Keeper Bess Harrowgate watched four separate parties argue over one shared supply of 900 torches, all of which appeared to be in all of their bags at once. By nightfall the pocket held, per one tally, 61 bedrolls, a dozen ladders, an unlicensed owlbear cub, and a ledger from Shieldwall Mutual denying coverage for exactly this. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said Chapter 9 considers the matter "on track" and has begun charging a retrieval fee.

Naturally the regulators are circling. Reeve Fennick said only, "We are aware of the pocket." I'd rather not comment on a body that thinks a 400-complaint rounding error needs a permit. Meanwhile, an unnamed shop steward at the Outfitters' Brindlemoor warehouse, one of those union types, has demanded hazard pay for staff who reach in to sort the returns. Fourteen of them have been rightsized to the other side of the bag, where, I'm told, the networking is excellent.

I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove once, at a spring gala in a hot-air balloon. He told me, "Sterling, never own what you can lease from a stranger's pocket." I have thought about it every morning since, during my sword routine.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A shared bag of holding is a community. Label your goat.
  • Disruption always starts with 412 complaints.
  • If it is in the pocket, it is liquid.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Mimic Posing as Tavern Door Swallows 31 Hats on Fish Street
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A mimic disguised as a tavern door on Fish Street ate 31 hats in three weeks before the Constabulary noticed. Skritch allegedly got his tail stuck.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight, the Constabulary was allegedly called to the Rusty Ladle on Fish Street, where a mimic had spent three weeks pretending to be the front door. By the Constabulary's count it ate 31 hats, one eyepatch, and a bard's second-best lute. Nobody noticed because the door, allegedly, always opened.

'I pushed on it every night,' said Gorbin Tuck, a cooper who was eating a pickled egg at the time. 'It felt sticky. I figured the damp.' Tuck lost a wool cap in the second week and blamed a draft.

The trouble started when regulars began going home bareheaded and, in several cases, without their pride. Barmaid Odalie Fenn says she noticed the hat pile was shrinking from the wrong end. 'Customers come in wearing hats. Customers leave not wearing hats. That's not a draft, that's a pattern,' she said, and then served me a very small beer. It was a nice mug, though. Copper rim.

Constabulary Sergeant Brindle Pamm says the mimic was found when a patron tried to leave through the door and the door tried to leave through the patron. 'It had a knocker and everything,' Pamm said. 'Hinges, too. Painted-on hinges. Very convincing hinges.' The patron, a halfling named Dob, was allegedly pulled free by his ankles and is expected to recover his dignity by spring.

I went to see it myself. Allegedly I did not touch the door. Reader, I touched the door. My left foot is still a little sticky and the mimic has, allegedly, my second-best boot. Ooh, also there was a very nice brass knocker lying right there, which I am told is the mimic's actual knocker. I have been told not to take it. Anyway.

The Rusty Ladle's owner, Hesk Varnow, says he installed the door in a hurry last month after a gelatinous mishap and never asked where it came from. 'It was cheap, and it matched the frame,' Varnow said. 'A good door should match the frame.' He has since moved the tavern entrance to a window.

The Constabulary has the mimic in a locked cellar on Tanner's Row, where it is allegedly pretending to be a crate. Wizards from the Tower District have offered to buy it, which tells you everything about the Tower District. The hats, the Constabulary says, will be returned in order of how digested they are.

Pigeons, I note, were seen on the roof the whole time and said nothing. Allegedly in on it.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Doppelganger Held Two Council Seats; Quorum Void
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A doppelganger sat as two members of Brindlemoor's Burgess Council for a year, so every quorum since is void. The Chamber took a recess to discuss it.
item.content:encoded:
The Burgess Council of Brindlemoor learned on Tuesday that a doppelganger has occupied two of its nine seats for roughly a year, which means no quorum call since last autumn was valid. The discovery came when the lady from the Tanner's Ward and the gentleman from the Candle Quarter were seen eating lunch together, in the same coat, from the same plate.

The Council requires seven members present to conduct business. By the clerk's reckoning, seven were present at every sitting, but one of the seven was always two of them. The true count was therefore six, and six is not a quorum under Standing Order 4. I checked. It is on page nine.

The doppelganger, who gave its name to the clerk as Burgess Orrin Tallowby and then, after a pause, as Burgess Wenna Tallowby, declined to speak to the gallery. Through counsel it said it had attended every sitting, read every bill, and voted consistently, which it noted put it ahead of the other seven.

The gentleman from the Cooper's Ward moved that the matter be referred to committee. The lady from the Weir Street Ward objected that the committee also contained the doppelganger. A recess was called. It lasted three hours, during which the Council could not formally agree that it was in recess.

The consequences are considerable. Every ordinance passed in twelve months is now of doubtful standing, including the owlbear leash ordinance, which passed 5-4 last week. The doppelganger voted for it twice. Without those votes it fails 3-4, though the owlbear in the gallery has said it considers the ordinance binding on everyone else regardless.

The clerk, Hobb Pennywhistle, produced the attendance book and showed that the doppelganger signed both names in different hands, one of them left-handed. "I assumed they were twins," he said. "Burgess Tallowby had mentioned a twin. Burgess Tallowby had mentioned a lot of things." Asked why he never raised it, Pennywhistle said nobody had asked him to count the people, only the signatures.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the doppelganger had in fact been the Council's most reliable member. It never missed a vote, never spoke past its allotted time, and was the only member to read the budget. "It was two of the best Burgesses we had," the courtier said. "We have now lost both."

The Council meets again Friday to decide whether Friday counts. By my tally this brings the session's Promises Made to nine, and Promises Kept to the one about holding lunch in public, which was kept more thoroughly than anyone intended. Three members have already announced they will contest the seat of the doppelganger, and one of them is the doppelganger.

The motion to adjourn carried 4-0. Nobody could say who had counted.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Autocorrect Wand Turns Fireball Into 'Fire Ball Pit'
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Brightkettle's new Smartcast wand has built-in autocorrect for incantations. Nyx tried a fireball and got a ball pit. Four eyes, singed.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. Brightkettle Wandworks launched the Smartcast wand on Tuesday, the first wand with autocorrect for incantations, and I was first in line at the Brindlemoor shop, which opened at nine and ran out of stock at nine-oh-one. The pitch is simple: mispronounce a word and the wand quietly fixes it before the magic goes off. I tested it on a fireball.

The runic latency is wonderful! I said "fireball" at a training dummy, the wand paused for a delicate half second, and the dummy was buried in several hundred bright foam spheres. A clerk at the shop later explained that the wand "learned" from the realm's most common casting phrases, and the word the realm says most near children is, apparently, "ball pit." Nobody was hurt. The dummy is thriving.

Other users have fared worse. Maribel Thornwhistle, a hedge-wizard from the east market, told me her wand changed "light" to "lightning" during a quiet supper. Her stew survived. The ceiling did not. A guard captain on night shift reports his wand rewrote "hold person" into "hold perception," and he has been unable to notice anything since Tuesday, which he says is the same as a normal shift.

Brightkettle's helpful assistant, a tiny spirit who lives in the grip and calls itself Quill, offers suggestions as you cast. "Did you mean: sleep?" it asks, mid-fireball. You can't dismiss it. Quill also wants a Premium tier at 6 gp a month to "stop suggesting." It is a subscription fee for silence, the worst category of fee, and I paid it twice because I lost the receipt.

The wand has an option called Predictive Casting, which finishes your incantation for you. It finished mine with a toast to the health of a distant cousin, at a funeral, aloud. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, now speaks only in ad copy and said, "Smartcast. Say less, mean more." This is both a slogan and a threat. Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to just speak clearly and touch grass. Brother Tumbleberry has never watched a wand finish his sentences in public, and I would sell my entire rune-chip collection to watch him try.

Brightkettle says a patch will ship "as soon as the wand is ready." Support suggests turning the wand off and on again, which in a wand means a short ritual, a candle, and a promise not to tell the wand about its mother.

Verdict: four out of five beholder eyes. The wand understands me better than I understand myself. Unfortunately, it keeps being wrong about it.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Burns sustained: 1. Ball pits conjured: 1. Subscription fees paid by mistake: 2. Eyebrows: pending.

item.title: Young Red Dragon Hoard Permit Approved, With Cheese Conditions
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Cellars Board approved a young red dragon's hoard extension under Tanner's Row, 4 votes to 1, on condition that the cheese is shared fairly.
item.content:encoded:
BRINDLEMOOR CELLARS BOARD HEARING ROOM, GROUND LEVEL (I checked) — The Cellars Board voted 4 to 1 last night to let Skorvath, the young red dragon, extend its hoard under three Tanner's Row cellars. The permit comes with eleven conditions. Seven concern cheese.

Skorvath's hoard of 11,400 gold pieces already lies beneath the old tannery. The extension adds roughly 3,000 square feet of floor and, the dragon's filing notes, 'no new fires.' It attended in person, folded into the back of the room, and stated for the record that the two earlier fires were 'a matter of record and a matter of regret.' Board Chair Tolly Wend gaveled it in. The gavel survived.

The vote turned on the cheese survey, which found the hoard's heat ripens cheddar in hours. Inspector Corwin Tallowby read the numbers aloud: a wheel that takes eleven months in a normal cellar takes under four hours at the edge of the pile. 'I have classified this as favorable,' Tallowby said. 'I have also classified my own surprise. It is on a separate form.'

The conditions, as filed: Skorvath may not sit on any wheel not its own. Cheese ripened in the hoard must be sold at posted prices, with a third of each batch set aside for the Board's tasting table. The dragon must keep a ten-foot pole's width between the pile and any cellar wall, and I have counted one pole lost to this beat already today. Cellar doors get two keys, one held by the keeper and one by the dragon, so that neither can claim surprise.

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, whose cellar is one of the three, did not oppose the permit. 'It pays rent in cheese,' she said. 'The cube paid in nothing.' She has agreed to a trial: forty wheels, one night, results tomorrow. Her cellar floor was dry-swept for the occasion.

The lone no vote came from Board member Hester Quillfoot, who owns a competing aging cave outside town and was asked to recuse herself. She declined, citing 'a deep personal interest in not being the slow option.' The Board noted the objection and moved on.

Reeve Fennick was seen leaving the hearing with a wedge of cheddar and no comment. When asked, the party's bard, who asked to be named, said he had 'a feeling about the cheese,' then ate it. Hit points at the hearing: Board, 5 of 5; dragon, full; Tallowby, full, except for his composure.

The extension begins at the next new moon. I rolled poorly on last week's cellar prediction, which said the permit would be tabled again, so take this one with a wedge of salt.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Bridge Troll Raises Toll to 3 Copper, Baronies Parley
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: A bridge troll raised the toll on Quillmarch Bridge from two copper to three, and two baronies sent envoys. Tension holds at nine siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
A bridge troll named Gorvash Pennyfist raised the toll on Quillmarch Bridge from two copper pieces to three on Fourthday. The barony of Ashenfold and the barony of Brackwater, who share the only crossing for forty miles, sent envoys to a parley by sundown.

The parley was held on the bridge itself, because the troll would not leave it. Gorvash sat on the east rail. Ashenfold's envoy stood at the west end. Brackwater's envoy stood at the east end, which put him next to the troll and visibly regretting it. The handshake between the two envoys lasted two seconds. Firm. No hidden dagger detected. One envoy did hide a pie, which was declared a field ration and allowed.

Gorvash read a statement. "Costs are up," he said. "Goats are up. Goats are up forty percent. I do not set the goats." Asked whether the third copper piece was a negotiating position, the troll said it was a copper piece. He then asked the envoys to move along, because they were blocking the queue.

The queue stretched back to a hamlet called Lower Dunmoor. Wagoners, a travelling cheesemonger, and a family of six with one very tired donkey waited in the rain while the envoys argued over the word "adjustment." Ashenfold calls the hike a tax. Brackwater calls it a fee. The troll calls it "a toll, like always," and has not moved from that position since he took the bridge nine winters ago.

Ashenfold's envoy, Dame Hesper Orlowe, demanded a return to two copper pieces and an independent audit of the goats. Brackwater's envoy, Sir Tobin Garrick, proposed that both baronies pay the extra copper piece out of a shared fund, which Ashenfold rejected because it had spent the fund on a fence. Brackwater then offered to build a second bridge. Gorvash said he would be glad to take the toll on that one too.

I have covered sieges that moved faster. I have covered a siege where the defenders ate the siege engines. Here nobody has a catapult, nobody has an army, and everybody has a very strong opinion about three coppers. The honest enemy on this bridge is the troll, and he is the only one who has told the truth all week. I respect it. I do not like it.

The ordinary traveller is the casualty, as ever. A shepherd named Edda told this paper she now walks the long way round, which adds two days and one copper piece's worth of blisters. Nobody in either barony has asked her what she thinks. The envoys did, however, issue a joint press release, which this correspondent has fed to the donkey.

The parley resumes at dawn. The troll will be on the rail. The toll stays at three until further notice. Tension holds at nine siege-days, and the goats remain unaudited.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Pit Trap Pay Strike: Undermaw Porters Walk Off the Job
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Sixty-one hireling porters stopped walking point in the Undermaw Tuesday. They want hazard pay for finding every pit trap with their feet.
item.content:encoded:
They put down the poles. Sixty-one hireling porters walked off the job Tuesday at the mouth of the Undermaw, demanding hazard pay for every pit trap they find the hard way. Chapter 9 pays them four silver a day to walk in front of adventuring parties. The porters say that works out to about one silver per fall.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick called the walkout 'a soft pause in our point-position pipeline.' That means nobody wants to go first. He added that Chapter 9 remains 'on track' and that no party has been left without a floor.

The floor is the problem. 'Level Three has forty-two pit traps on the official map,' said Dunmar Quillfoot, a ten-foot-pole bearer for eleven years. 'I've found thirty-nine of them. The map is wrong about the other three, and so is my left knee.' Quillfoot held up a pole worn to a stub. Chapter 9 issues one per season. It deducts the cost of the replacement from his wages.

Hazard pay is the whole demand. The porters also want a proper lunch break, which at present is whenever the party stops screaming, and a rope at the top of every pit they fall into. 'Just a rope,' said Odalie Burrowgate, a lantern carrier. 'Not a good rope. A rope that's there.'

Chapter 9 says it offered a package. The package, read aloud at the picket line by Quillfoot, includes a free hat, a 'resilience workshop,' and an annual Fall Appreciation Day. Fall Appreciation Day is held at the bottom of the pit on Level Two. Nobody laughed. Burrowgate said she had been to the workshop and it was in the pit.

Parties are already feeling it. The Fourth Attempt, licensed to delve Wednesday, sent its own wizard in front with a feather fall spell and a very worried face. 'He's a specialist,' said a spokesman for the party. 'We value his contributions.' The wizard was heard to say that he had not been asked.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said the town is 'aware of the pits' and urged both sides to talk. She also asked adventurers to stop sending their cousins down as replacements. Eight cousins have fallen so far. Six of them are fine and two have joined the union.

Meanwhile Chapter 9 posted a notice on its door seeking 'enthusiastic point-position volunteers, no experience needed, experience not expected.' That is the guild's way of hiring a person to fall down a hole for free. Not one porter has crossed the line, and Quillfoot says the pits will keep.

Bring snacks to the picket if you can. They're out there in the mud, and nobody's falling.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Rust Monster Eats 9,000 gp of Iron Pennies at Mint
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A rust monster ate 9,000 gp of iron pennies at the Brindlemoor mint on Tuesday, and small change is already scarce. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
A rust monster wandered into the Brindlemoor mint on Tuesday and ate roughly 9,000 gp worth of iron pennies, leaving the town with a shortage of small change. Mint officials say the creature came in through the delivery door behind a cart of ingots and was not noticed until the ingots were gone, followed by the cart's axles.

The sum is 30,000 loaves on the current Loaf Index. (I have checked this four times, and a fifth time while eating toast, which felt disrespectful.) That is a great deal of bread to lose to one animal that, by every account, looked pleased with itself afterward.

The Master of the Mint, Hobart Quillfeather, told reporters the stock was meant for the autumn change run, when taverns and bakeries need pennies for the harvest crowds. "We had every penny counted," he said. "Then it was a different number." Quillfeather confirmed that gold and silver were untouched, as the rust monster has no interest in them, and that the mint's remaining copper is now being guarded by a retired watchman with a wooden spoon.

The economics underneath are simpler than they look. Small coins circulate fast. When the supply drops, shops round prices up to the next silver piece because nobody can make change, and a bread that cost seven pennies starts costing ten. Baker Edda Longbottom said she raised her loaf by a penny out of necessity, "and then another one out of principle." By Wednesday, three stalls on Market Row were refusing change altogether and writing "keep the rest, please" on their signs.

Quillfeather says the mint will restamp pennies from copper by the end of next week, using a mending casting to repair what the rust monster only half chewed. The apprentice assigned to the task asked that the creature be removed from the building first, a request the mint called reasonable.

Sterling Vanmoor called the incident "a healthy reset for the penny sector." I would like Mr. Vanmoor to try buying one apple with a silver piece and see how much of the apple he gets back. Meanwhile, the creature has been moved to a stable outside town, where it is eating the gate.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, notes that her boot is leather and therefore of no interest to the monster. She has asked me not to say where it is. What this means for your pantry: carry exact change, and buy your bread before the baker does the arithmetic.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Potion of Healing Labels Must List Side Effects, Guild Rules
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Marrowfield Apothecaries' Guild now requires every potion of healing to list dosage and side effects. The label is bigger than the vial.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the Marrowfield Apothecaries' Guild voted 31 to 4 on Monday to make every potion of healing carry a label listing its dose, its side effects, and what not to drink it with. A fair idea, I say. The trouble is that the first labels run to fourteen inches and the vials are three.

Guildmaster Tamsin Applewick held up a sample at the vote. It wound around the vial six times and then trailed to the floor like a bride's veil. "We have been very thorough," she said. "The warnings include itchy ears, brief singing, and an urge to hug a goat."

The old herbals have always said a medicine should come with plain advice: take it with food, take it after rest, and do not take it at all if you are cross with your mother. And here, for once, is an actual study. A small trial at the Marrowfield infirmary found patients read a short label twice as often as a long one, and a long one hardly at all. I am sorry to say that our healers ran the numbers and found that nobody finishes a fourteen-inch label.

Apothecary Dunmore Greywether, who stocks the biggest shelf in the market, says the new labels have slowed his work. "I have to hire a boy just to unroll them," he told me. "Yesterday a customer sneezed and the label wound itself around his leg."

I did ask the Guild whether a short label might do the job. A clerk told me the Guild is studying the question, and has produced a report on it that is fourteen inches long. I did not read it, friends, and I suspect the report knew.

So here is what I suggest while the Guild finds its scissors. Ask your apothecary the three plain questions: what is it for, how much, and what happens if I take too much? If they cannot answer in one breath, ask for a different apothecary. And never mix a potion with ale, no matter what your cousin says.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there is an app that reads labels aloud. Go outside, Nyx, and read the label on a tree.

Tonight I recommend a plain chicken-and-rice soup, which has a label of exactly one line: chicken, rice, water.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Gelatinous Cube Replaces 40 Dishwashers at Tavern Chain
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Tankard & Crumb Taverns laid off 40 dishwashers and installed one gelatinous cube in the scullery. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a bold pivot.
item.content:encoded:
Tankard & Crumb Taverns announced Monday that it has laid off 40 dishwashers across its six Hollowpeck locations and replaced them with a single gelatinous cube. The cube is housed in the central scullery and reportedly cleans 900 plates an hour. I call this rightsizing the adventuring party, and frankly, it is the most elegant cost line I have seen all year.

Chief Executive Hob Fennimore unveiled the hire at a breakfast presentation, standing beside the cube in a freshly pressed tabard. "Our new colleague has no sick days, no wage demands, and a remarkable work ethic," he said. "He also absorbs the plates, but we see that as a feature we can scale." The cube has not yet been given a name, only a badge number.

Early results are strong. Tankard & Crumb reports a 62% drop in labor costs and a 100% drop in lingering grease. A few teething issues remain. The cube has dissolved 31 forks, a ladle, and one regional manager's notebook, which the company describes as "an unscheduled data cleanse."

Former dishwasher Pip Larkwater, 29, was less enthusiastic. "I washed those plates for six years," he said, outside the scullery door. "The cube eats the plates." The Servers' Benevolent Lodge has called for a picket. I call that classic union energy: refusing to see that an ooze is simply a more motivated team member.

When I met Guildmaster Dagmar Coldpenny at a gala years ago, she told me, "Sterling, the best employee is the one who cannot read a contract." I think about that every morning during my sword routine. The cube cannot read. The cube also cannot be sued, though a stable boy tried on its behalf.

Fennimore says a second cube is planned for the pantry, subject to a successful pilot and a very large net. Shares of Tankard & Crumb rose 4% on the news. Diners were less moved, mostly because they were still looking for their spoons.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

- Automation is just a coworker with fewer questions.
- Always keep your notebook out of the scullery.
- A layoff is a pivot if you say it with a smile.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.
